lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.unitTitle: Systems of Linear Equations and Inequalities
lessonRef.focus: proving that replacement by a sum preserves the solution set
lessonRef.title: Launch and diagnostic: proving that replacement by a sum preserves the solution set

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Read the example first. You are not expected to know this yet.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Try each one. If you get stuck, write what you do know and move on.

items.prompt:
How many solutions does this system have?
  -2x + 2y = -6
  -8x + 8y = -19
choices: infinitely many solutions
no solution
exactly two solutions
exactly one solution

items.prompt: Is the point (-4, -3) in the solution region of 2x + 3y ≤ 7?
choices: The region cannot be tested without graphing it first.
Yes; substituting gives -17 ≤ 7.
Only points on the boundary line are in the solution region.
No; substituting gives -17, which is greater than 7.

items.prompt: A student replaces the second equation of a system with (second equation) + 2 × (first equation). Which statement is correct?
choices: The new system may gain solutions that the original did not have.
The new system has exactly the same solution set, because the replacement step is reversible.
The new system may lose solutions that the original had.
The new system is equivalent only when 2 is 1.

sections.title: Mastery check
sections.directions: Show what you can do so far. This sets the starting point, not a grade.

items.prompt:
How many solutions does this system have?
  4x + 5y = -3
  8x + 10y = -1
choices: infinitely many solutions
no solution
exactly one solution
exactly two solutions

items.prompt: Is the point (-1, 1) in the solution region of 3x − 4y ≤ -6?
choices: The region cannot be tested without graphing it first.
Only points on the boundary line are in the solution region.
Yes; substituting gives -7 ≤ -6.
No; substituting gives -7, which is greater than -6.
